# Market Street Saturday pilot: brief

## Assignment

- Mode: adapt
- Format: 45-second elevator speech without slides
- Audience: city councillors
- Decision point: the 4 December session
- Tone: direct, constructive and easy to repeat
- Speaker details were not provided, so the script uses no personal story or identity-specific claim.

## Goal

The city council approves a three-month pilot closing Market Street to cars on Saturdays.

## Message

Give Market Street back to people on Saturdays.

## Argument

**Local shops.** Many local shops have backed the idea. The supplied proof is the traders’ association survey, in which 70 percent were in favour.

This is the sole argument because an elevator speech of 60 seconds or less allows one argument. It is also the only argument supplied with quantitative proof.

## Elephant

Councillors may ask about traffic and access. The input contains no operational plan, so those questions are parked in the Q&A preparation and must be answered with verified information rather than guesses.

## Structure

1. Hook and problem: cars currently get Market Street on Saturdays.
2. Solution: a three-month Saturday pilot.
3. One proof: 70 percent in favour in the traders’ association survey.
4. Ask: vote yes at the 4 December session.

## Timing

78 spoken words ÷ 130 words per minute × 60 = **36.0 seconds**. There are no timed long pauses. The delivery limit is **40.5 seconds**, or 90 percent of the 45-second slot.

## Accuracy

The main speech uses only the supplied facts. It contains no unresolved source gaps. Missing evidence for possible council questions is identified in `rehearsal.md`.

# Market Street Saturdays: script

78 words = 36.0 s · 0 long pauses = 0 s · total 36.0 s · limit 40.5 s (90% of 45 s)

`/` = short pause · **bold** = stress

## Opening: hook and problem (0:00–0:06)

[MEMORIZE] Cars get Market Street on Saturdays. / Give Market Street back to people on Saturdays. /

## Solution (0:06–0:19)

[MEMORIZE] Start with a three-month pilot: close it to cars for that one day each week. /

Then people can stop, meet and shop, instead of fitting around traffic. /

## One proof: local shops (0:19–0:27)

Many local shops have already backed that idea: the traders’ association survey found **70 percent** in favour. /

## Ask (0:27–0:36)

[MEMORIZE] Councillors, at the 4 December session, **vote yes** on the pilot—and give Market Street back to people on Saturdays.

## Alternative openings

Each option replaces the 14-word opening above; all remain within the timing limit.

- **Connect — 15 words; full script 79 words = 36.5 s:** “Our streets show what our city values. / Give Market Street back to people on Saturdays.”
- **Engage — 18 words; full script 82 words = 37.8 s:** “Who should Market Street serve on Saturdays: cars or people? / Give Market Street back to people on Saturdays.”
- **Surprise — recommended; 14 words; full script 78 words = 36.0 s:** “Cars get Market Street on Saturdays. / Give Market Street back to people on Saturdays.”

# Market Street Saturdays: cue cards

## Card 1: Opening [0:00]

“Cars get Market Street on Saturdays.
Give Market Street back to people on Saturdays.”

## Card 2: Solution [0:06]

- three-month pilot
- Saturdays: close to cars
- one day each week
- stop · meet · shop
- contrast: fitting around traffic

## Card 3: Local shops [0:19]

- traders’ association survey
- **70% in favour**
- many local shops backed it
- bridge: “Councillors…”

## Card 4: Ask [0:27]

“Councillors, at the 4 December session,
vote yes on the pilot—and give Market Street
back to people on Saturdays.”

## Card 5: After Q&A

“Local shops have already backed this idea:
the traders’ association survey found 70 percent in favour.
For one day each week, let people stop, meet and shop.
Give Market Street back to people on Saturdays.
At the 4 December session, vote yes on the three-month pilot.”

# Market Street Saturdays: rehearsal kit

## Timing

| Section | Starts | Lasts | Words | Pauses | Skip if late? |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Hook and problem | 0:00 | 6.5 s | 14 | 2 short | No |
| Solution | 0:06 | 12.5 s | 27 | 2 short | No |
| Local-shop proof | 0:19 | 7.8 s | 17 | 1 short | No |
| Ask | 0:27 | 9.2 s | 20 | — | No |
| **Total** |  | **36.0 s** | **78** | **0 timed** |  |

The formal limit is 40.5 seconds. Aim for 38–40 seconds in rehearsal once the short pauses are included.

## Practice plan

1. Read the speech aloud once and simplify any phrase that catches.
2. Memorize the first three sentences and the final CTA word for word.
3. Give three timed runs. Keep every run at or below 40.5 seconds without rushing.
4. Record the last run. Check that “70 percent” and “vote yes” are clear, and that the final line does not trail off.
5. Ask someone outside council work to repeat the message and the requested action.

## Top three techniques

1. **Pause after the message and the survey result.** A short beat lets each memorable line land without consuming the elevator-length time budget.
2. **Stress the decision words.** Emphasize “70 percent,” “4 December” and “vote yes”; keep the surrounding words conversational.
3. **Use lighthouse eye contact.** Hold one councillor per thought, then address the full council for the CTA. Stay planted rather than pacing during this short speech.

## Q&A preparation

1. **Numbers: How reliable is the 70 percent figure?**  
   “The figure comes from the traders’ association survey: 70 percent were in favour. I would not claim more without [NEEDS SOURCE: sample size, field dates, exact question, respondent definition, response rate and sampling method]. That is the evidence behind giving Market Street back to people on Saturdays.”

2. **Hardest question: What if shops lose trade?**  
   “I do not have outcome data and will not promise a result. Judge the pilot using [NEEDS SOURCE: baseline and pilot sales or footfall measurement plan]. The evidence supplied today is that 70 percent in the traders’ association survey were in favour.”

3. **What will the pilot cost?**  
   “The verified figure is [NEEDS SOURCE: itemised pilot cost, funding source and staffing requirement]. I will not guess at it. With that checked, my ask remains a yes vote on 4 December.”

4. **Elephant: Where will displaced traffic go?**  
   “That must be answered from [NEEDS SOURCE: traffic-diversion plan, modelling and monitoring arrangements]. I will not invent a route. The aim remains to give Market Street back to people on Saturdays.”

5. **How will deliveries and business access work?**  
   “The operating details must come from [NEEDS SOURCE: delivery, servicing and business-access plan, including hours]. They should support the Saturday pilot without unsupported promises.”

6. **How will people with limited mobility reach the street?**  
   “The answer must follow [NEEDS SOURCE: verified accessibility and mobility-access plan]. That plan should make giving Market Street back to people genuinely inclusive.”

7. **What about emergency services and public transport?**  
   “Use [NEEDS SOURCE: emergency-service access arrangements and any public-transport changes or approvals]. I will not speculate; those arrangements must support the Saturday pilot.”

8. **How will the council decide whether the pilot worked?**  
   “Use [NEEDS SOURCE: success measures, baseline, measurement owner, reporting date and post-pilot decision process]. The council should judge the three-month pilot from evidence.”

9. **Why Saturdays, and why three months?**  
   “The brief specifies both but gives no rationale. Have [NEEDS SOURCE: verified rationale for Saturday closures and the three-month duration]. The decision requested on 4 December is approval of that pilot.”

## Final close after Q&A

Local shops have already backed this idea: the traders’ association survey found 70 percent in favour. For one day each week, let people stop, meet and shop. Give Market Street back to people on Saturdays. At the 4 December session, vote yes on the three-month pilot.

## Day-of check

- Bring the survey source and the verified Q&A evidence.
- Run the opening and CTA once with a timer.
- Keep notes to keywords; do not read the body.
- Finish on “vote yes on the three-month pilot”—do not add “thank you.”
